content: In individuals with asthma, several physiological factors can contribute to lung hyperinflation. These include expiratory airflow limitation, premature closure of small airways, persistent activity of inspiratory muscles at the end of expiration, and reduced pulmonary compliance. As lung volume increases, the geometry of the chest wall is altered, leading to a shortening of the inspiratory muscles. This places the muscles in a suboptimal position within their length-tension relationship, thereby reducing their ability to generate tension effectively. However, hypertrophy of the inspiratory muscles, which increases their cross-sectional area, may counteract this functional weakening caused by hyperinflation. Previous research has demonstrated that inspiratory muscle training (IMT) can induce diaphragm hypertrophy in both healthy individuals and patients with chronic heart failure. Additionally, in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), IMT has been shown to increase the proportion of type I muscle fibers and the size of type II fibers in the external intercostal muscles. Despite these findings, the effects of IMT on clinical outcomes in individuals with asthma remain unclear. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of inspiratory muscle training, using either an external resistive device or threshold loading, in individuals with asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register of trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and ClinicalTrials.gov. The search was last updated in November 2012. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving the use of an external inspiratory muscle training device compared to a control (sham device or no training) in individuals with stable asthma were included in the analysis. Five studies, involving a total of 113 adult participants, were included in the review. Four of these studies focused on individuals with mild to moderate asthma, while the fifth study included participants regardless of asthma severity. The studies varied significantly in their training protocols, with session durations ranging from 10 to 30 minutes and intervention periods lasting between 3 and 25 weeks. Notably, three of the trials were conducted by the same research group. The risk of bias in the included studies was challenging to assess due to inadequate reporting of methodological details. The results indicated a statistically significant improvement in inspiratory muscle strength, as measured by maximal inspiratory pressure (PImax), with a mean difference of 13.34 cmH2O (95% confidence interval: 4.70 to 21.98) based on data from four studies involving 84 participants. However, the quality of evidence was rated as low. The primary outcome of asthma exacerbations requiring oral or inhaled corticosteroids or emergency department visits was not reported in any of the studies. For secondary outcomes, one trial reported no statistically significant differences between the IMT group and the control group in terms of maximal expiratory pressure, peak expiratory flow rate, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), sensation of dyspnoea, or use of beta2-agonists. Additionally, no studies reported on inspiratory muscle endurance, hospital admissions, or days missed from work or school. In conclusion, this review found no definitive evidence to either support or refute the use of inspiratory muscle training for asthma. The findings were limited by the small number of trials, the low number of participants, and the potential risk of bias. Further well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate the effects of IMT on outcomes such as lung function, exacerbation rates, asthma symptoms, hospital admissions, medication use, and days missed from work or school. Future research should also explore the efficacy of IMT in individuals with more severe asthma and in children with asthma.
